prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Elasticity and Strength of Materials

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling learning new methods and theories, and providing versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to deepen the analysis of a specific scientific-technological problem, analyze it, identify the problem and provide a solution proposal.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity and critical reasoning.
Ability to manage mandatory specifications, regulations and standards.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of Fracture Mechanics, both in written and oral form, and to all types of audiences.
Ability to prepare and publicly defend a research paper on a specific problem in Fracture Mechanics.
Ability to evaluate the structural integrity of components subjected to the action of mechanical loads.

Ability to understand the behavior of different cracked mechanical components or components with stress concentrators, considering factors such as the type of applied load, their geometry, the type of material they are made of, or the type of environment in which they must perform their service.
Ability to improve the fracture behavior of an element in order to obtain novel products or products with better performance.
Ability to manage existing regulations and equipment for performing the most commonly used mechanical tests in the fracture characterization of mechanical elements.

Ability to use the most advanced engineering methodologies, techniques, skills and tools (numerical calculation, statistical methods, etc.) in order to improve conventional designs and obtain optimal solutions.
Ability to manage different resources and technologies that allow obtaining updated scientific information on the research topic to be developed.
Knowledge and use of the principles of Fracture Mechanics.

To know the behavior of different cracked mechanical components and components with stress concentrators considering factors such as the type of applied load, their geometry, the type of material they are made of or the environment in which they must perform their service.
To know how to alter factors such as the geometry of the element or the type of material it is made of to improve its failure behavior.
To know how to analyze the safety of cracked components and components with stress concentrators subjected to mechanical and thermal loads.
To know the existing standardized tests to characterize the behavior of materials in the presence of cracks.
To know the behavior laws of materials under different situations and loading modes.
To know the methodology for carrying out fracture tests.
To know and apply the different criteria for calculating fracture toughness, both static and dynamic.
To develop structural elements with better failure behavior through modification of their geometry and selection of the most suitable material.
Ability to quantify the safety of cracked components and components with stress concentrators under actual service loads.

To handle the scientific equipment necessary to carry out the fracture characterization of cracked mechanical elements and elements with stress concentrators under the conditions analyzed in the course.
To organize a specific work and carry it out individually and/or in a group.
To write a scientific paper in a summarized way.
To foster an observational and analytical character in the student.
To create a research interest in the student.
To provide the student with an organizational and participatory sense for carrying out both individual and group work.
Formation of an open, critical and entrepreneurial spirit.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to fracture mechanics: Concept of structural integrity. Conventional calculation concept versus fracture calculation concept. Concept of fracture toughness. Loading modes. Historical perspective and social impact. Types of fracture.

Linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM). Energy criterion for fracture. Stress analysis. Stress intensity factor: Experimental and numerical calculation. Relationship between G and K. Mixed mode. Stress criterion for fracture. Plasticity at the crack front and validity conditions for LEFM. Tests for determining fracture toughness in different materials. Biparametric LEFM. Biaxial stress states. The T-stress and biaxiality parameter. R-curves: Fracture criterion.

Elastoplastic fracture mechanics (EPFM). General concepts. The CTOD parameter: Experimental determination and design curves based on CTOD. The J-integral: J as an energy parameter, J as a contour integral, and J as a stress parameter. HRR fields. Experimental determination of J. Relationship between J and CTOD. Resistance to crack growth: J-R curves. Standardized tests. Application of the J-integral to structural calculation: EPRI procedure. Limitations of elastoplastic fracture mechanics. Biparametric EPFM: The Q parameter.

Micromechanisms of fracture and material toughness. Mechanistic interpretation of fracture toughness. Micromechanisms of ductile and brittle fracture. Nucleation, growth, and coalescence of microvoids. Cleavage fracture and theoretical cleavage stress. Ductile-brittle transition curve. Microstructural factors influencing material toughness. Relationship between micromechanisms of failure and fracture mechanics parameters.
assessment_rules: To pass the course in the ordinary call, a minimum score of 4 out of 10 in the final theoretical-practical exam is mandatory. There is no minimum score required for laboratory reports or short assessment tests. If all established minimums are met, the final grade is calculated as (0.6 x PF) + (0.20 x PL) + (0.2 x PB). Otherwise, the qualification will be the minimum between the calculated score and 4.0. A final grade equal to or greater than 5 out of 10 is required to pass the course.
